entries.title: Replacement cost vs. actual cash value
entries.caption:
Two policies can cover the same couch and pay very different amounts. The difference often comes down to two phrases. 🛋️

REPLACEMENT COST coverage is designed to pay what it costs to replace a damaged item with a new one of similar kind and quality. ACTUAL CASH VALUE pays what the item was worth at the time of the loss, which means depreciation for age and wear is subtracted. On older belongings, that gap can be big.

Many home policies handle the house itself and your personal belongings differently, so it's worth checking both. Some policies also pay actual cash value first and the rest once the item is actually replaced.

entries.title: Renting? Your landlord's policy isn't yours
entries.caption:
One of the most common renter surprises: "I figured the landlord's insurance would cover it." 🏢

Your landlord's policy is generally built to protect the building and the landlord's own liability, not your personal belongings. If a fire, burst pipe or break-in damages your furniture, electronics or clothes, that's typically where renters insurance comes in.

Many renters policies also include personal liability, which can help if someone is hurt in your unit or you accidentally damage someone else's property, and additional living expenses if a covered loss forces you to stay somewhere else for a while.

Renting and not sure what you'd be covered for? Call or text (425) 419-0099 and we'll walk through it.

Coverage varies by policy, state and eligibility.

entries.title: What if the other driver has no insurance?
entries.caption:
You can drive carefully and still get hit by someone with little or no insurance. That's exactly the gap uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage is designed for. 🚗

UNINSURED motorist coverage can help pay for your injuries, and in some cases damage to your car, when the at-fault driver has no insurance or it's a hit-and-run. UNDERINSURED motorist coverage can help when the at-fault driver has insurance, but not enough to cover your costs.

What's included, and whether it covers injuries, vehicle damage or both, depends on your policy and your state.

Want to know if you have it and how much? Call or text (425) 419-0099 for a quick review.

entries.title: Make a home inventory before you need one
entries.caption:
If you had to list everything in your home after a fire or break-in, how much would you forget? Most people forget a lot. 📱

A home inventory makes a claim faster and less stressful, and it helps you see whether your personal property limit is high enough. The easy version takes about 20 minutes:
• Record a slow video walking through every room
• Open closets, cabinets and drawers, and don't skip the garage
• Talk through bigger items as you go (brand, roughly when you bought it)
• Snap photos of receipts or serial numbers for electronics and jewelry
• Save it to cloud storage or email it to yourself so it survives if your home doesn't

Got your inventory and want to make sure your coverage matches it? Call or text (425) 419-0099.

entries.title: How much life insurance is enough?
entries.caption:
"How much life insurance do I need?" There's no one-size answer, but there is a simple way to start thinking about it. 💡

Many people begin by adding up what their family would need if their income stopped:
• Debts that would still need paying, including the mortgage
• Years of income your family would need replaced
• Future goals, like college for the kids
• Final expenses
Then subtract savings and any coverage you already have, like a policy through work.

It's a starting point, not a formula. Your real number depends on your goals, your budget and the people who rely on you. This post is educational only. Want to talk it through? Call or text (425) 419-0099.

entries.title: Frozen pipes: is the water damage covered?
entries.caption:
Freezing nights are on the way. Is your home policy ready for a burst pipe? 🧊

Most home policies treat water damage based on HOW it happened. A pipe that freezes and suddenly bursts is often considered sudden and accidental damage, which many policies cover. Water damage from a slow leak that went on for weeks, or from a pipe that froze because the home wasn't kept heated, is often treated as a maintenance issue and may be excluded.

A few simple habits help:
• Keep the heat at 55°F or higher, even when you travel
• Open cabinet doors under sinks on exterior walls
• Disconnect garden hoses and cover outdoor spigots
• Know where your main water shutoff is

Not sure how your policy handles water damage? Call or text (425) 419-0099 for a free coverage review.

Coverage varies by policy, state and eligibility.

entries.title: A windstorm drops a tree on your car. Now what?
entries.caption:
Storm season in the Northwest means falling branches. If one lands on your parked car, which part of your auto policy steps in? 🌲

Damage from things like falling trees, hail, flooding, fire, theft and hitting an animal generally falls under COMPREHENSIVE coverage. Collision is for when your car hits another vehicle or an object, like a guardrail. And if you only carry liability coverage, damage to your own car usually isn't covered at all.

Comprehensive typically has its own deductible, so check what yours is before the next windstorm, not after.

Want a quick look at what your auto policy includes? Call or text (425) 419-0099.

entries.title: Tree down in the yard? It depends what it hit
entries.caption:
After a windstorm, one of the most common questions is: "A tree came down. Is that covered?" The answer usually depends on what the tree hit. 🌬️

If a tree falls on your house, garage or another covered structure, the damage to that structure is often covered under your home policy, and some policies also help with removing the tree. If the tree falls in the yard without damaging anything, removal often isn't covered, or is covered only up to a small limit. And if a tree was dead or decaying beforehand, coverage can get more complicated.

Worth knowing before the next storm: how your policy handles debris removal and whether there's a cap on it.

entries.title: Term vs. permanent life, in plain English
entries.caption:
Life insurance comes in two main families, and the names don't always make it obvious which is which. 💡

TERM life covers you for a set number of years, often 10, 20 or 30. If you pass away during that term, your beneficiaries receive the death benefit. It's built to protect people during the years they depend on you most, like while kids are young or a mortgage is being paid down.

PERMANENT life (such as whole life) is designed to last your whole life and typically builds cash value over time, which is one reason it generally costs more.

Neither one is "better." The right fit depends on how long you need coverage and what you want it to do. This post is educational only. Want to talk through which type fits your situation? Call or text (425) 419-0099.

entries.title: What Your Deductible Really Means
entries.script: If you picked your car insurance deductible just to lower the price, this one's for you. Your deductible is what you pay out of pocket on a covered claim before insurance pays the rest. With a five hundred dollar deductible and a three thousand dollar covered repair, you pay the first five hundred and your policy handles the other twenty-five hundred. Here's the trade-off. A higher deductible usually lowers your premium, because you're taking on more of the risk. A lower deductible usually costs more, but hurts less when something happens. There's no perfect number. So here's your self-check. If you had a claim tomorrow, could you comfortably pay your deductible? If not, it might be time to revisit it. Next time, I'll break down the three numbers on your liability coverage, and why they matter. Insurance in Laymens terms.
entries.caption:
Your deductible is more than a number that changes your price. Here's what it really means when you file a claim, and a quick self-check to see if yours still fits.

entries.title: Slid on ice into a guardrail? That's collision
entries.caption:
Icy mornings are coming. If your car slides into a guardrail, a fence or another vehicle, here's how the coverage usually breaks down. ❄️

Damage to YOUR car from hitting something is typically handled by COLLISION coverage, after your deductible. Damage you cause to someone else's property, like their car or a guardrail, is generally handled by the property damage portion of your LIABILITY coverage. If you only carry liability, the repairs to your own car usually come out of your pocket.

Best protection is still prevention: slow down, leave extra space, and keep your tires in good shape.

Not sure whether you carry collision? Call or text (425) 419-0099 and we'll take a look.

Coverage varies by policy, state and eligibility.

entries.title: Run a business from home? Check this gap
entries.caption:
Working from home or running a side business out of the house? Your homeowners policy may not cover as much as you'd think. 🏠💼

Many home policies put a low limit on business equipment and inventory kept at home, and they often exclude liability that comes from business activities. So if a client trips on your front steps during a business visit, or your work laptop and inventory are stolen, your home policy might cover only a small part of it, or none at all.

Depending on the business, options like a home business endorsement or a business owner's policy (BOP) can help fill that gap.

entries.title: What an umbrella policy actually does
entries.caption:
An umbrella policy sounds fancy, but the idea is simple: it's extra liability protection that sits on top of your home and auto policies. ☂️

If you're found responsible for a serious accident or injury and the costs go past the liability limits on your home or auto policy, an umbrella policy can help pay the difference, up to its own limit. It can also cover some situations your other policies don't.

Umbrella coverage is worth a look if you own a home, have teen drivers, have a pool or trampoline, host often, or simply have savings and future earnings to protect.

entries.title: The Three Numbers on Your Liability Coverage
entries.script: Last time we covered deductibles. Today, let's decode the three numbers on your auto liability coverage. You'll usually see something like one hundred, three hundred, one hundred, in thousands of dollars. The first number is the most your policy pays for injuries to one person in an accident you cause. The second is the most it pays for all injuries in that accident combined. The third is the most it pays for damage to other people's property, like their car or their fence. Here's why it matters. If the costs of an accident you cause go past those limits, you could be responsible for the rest. So, self-check. Do you know your three numbers? Pull up your policy tonight and look. Next time, I'll explain comprehensive versus collision, and which one covers what. Insurance in Laymens terms.

Those three numbers on your auto policy, like 100/300/100, decide how protected you are if you cause an accident. Here's what each one means in plain English.
